questions.q: Fill up: Dizygotic twins form when ______, whereas monozygotic twins form when ______.
opts: 2 ova fertilized by 2 different sperms; 1 ovum fertilized by 1 sperm that then divides into 2
1 ovum fertilized by 1 sperm that then divides into 2; 2 ova fertilized by 2 different sperms
1 ovum fertilized by 2 different sperms; 2 separate ova fusing together after fertilisation
2 separate ova fusing together; 1 ovum fertilized by 2 different sperms after ovulation
questions.exp: Dizygotic twins form when 2 ova are fertilized by 2 different sperms, whereas monozygotic twins form when a single ovum fertilized by a single sperm divides into 2. (Book p460)

questions.q: Fill up: The more common twin type is ______ twins, also called ______ twins.
questions.exp: Dizygotic twins are more common and are called fraternal; monozygotic are identical. (Book p460)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about monozygotic twins is TRUE?
opts: Monozygotic twins share sex, blood group, HLA and phenotype, but fingerprints differ due to environment
Monozygotic twins share sex alone, since blood groups and HLA types always differ between them
Monozygotic twins share blood group alone, because sex and HLA can differ even in identical twins
Monozygotic twins share nothing, since they differ genetically as much as any two siblings
questions.exp: Monozygotic twins share the whole genome, so sex, blood groups, HLA and phenotype match; fingerprints differ because they are formed by the environment. (Book p460)

questions.q: Match the country with dizygotic twinning incidence — 1) Nigeria 2) Japan 3) India … A) 1 in 20 maximum B) 1 in 200 least C) 1 in 80
questions.exp: Incidence: Nigeria 1:20 max, Japan 1:200 least, India 1:80. (Book p460)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about monozygotic twinning incidence is TRUE?
opts: Monozygotic twinning incidence is uniform worldwide at about 1 in 250 births
Monozygotic twinning incidence is highest in Nigeria at 1 in 20 births overall
Monozygotic twinning incidence is lowest in Japan at 1 in 200 births worldwide
Monozygotic twinning incidence in India equals dizygotic twinning at 1 in 80 births
questions.exp: Monozygotic twinning is uniform worldwide (1 in 250). (Book p460)

questions.q: Fill up: As per Hellin's rule, if twins occur 1 in 80, triplets occur 1 in ______ and quadruplets 1 in ______.
questions.exp: Hellin's rule: triplets 1 in 80² and quadruplets 1 in 80³. (Book p460)

questions.q: Match the mechanism with its description — 1) Dizygotic twinning 2) Monozygotic twinning 3) Superfetation … A) One fertilised ovum splits, so the rate is constant across populations and the babies are genetically identical B) Two ova are fertilised, so the rate varies with maternal age, parity, race and ovulation induction C) A second conception occurs in a later cycle after a pregnancy is already established
questions.exp: Dizygotic rates vary with maternal factors and treatment; monozygotic splitting is a constant background event; superfetation is extremely rare. (Book p460)

questions.q: Fill up: Two ova released in the same cycle but fertilized at different times by different acts of coitus is ______ and it is ______ in humans.
questions.exp: Superfecundation = same-cycle ova fertilized at different times; it is rare but possible in humans. (Book p461)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about superfetation is TRUE?
opts: Superfetation is not seen in humans; theoretically possible only until cavity obliterated at 14-16 weeks
Superfetation is common after IVF when several embryos are transferred in one cycle
Superfetation is seen only in multiparous women who have a larger uterine cavity volume
Superfetation is the same as superfecundation where two ova of one cycle are fertilised
questions.exp: Superfetation would need a second ovulation and fertilisation after a pregnancy is established, which the decidua prevents. (Book p461)

questions.q: All of the following are recognised risk factors for dizygotic twinning EXCEPT:
opts: IVF as the sole risk factor with no role for geography, age, parity or family history at all
Geographical distribution with Nigeria showing highest incidence at 1 in 20 and Japan lowest
Advanced maternal age and increased parity raising chance of multiple ovulation and twins
Maternal family history of twins and ovulation-induction drugs like clomiphene and hMG
questions.exp: Dizygotic risks: geography, ↑ age, ↑ parity, maternal family history, IVF and ovulation induction; IVF alone is the monozygotic risk. (Book p461)

questions.q: The only listed risk factor for MONOZYGOTIC twins is:
questions.exp: Monozygotic twinning risk lists IVF only. (Book p461)

questions.q: Fill up: Zygosity refers to ______ while chorionicity refers to ______.
opts: type of conception; type of placentation
type of placentation; type of conception
number of sacs; number of embryos
questions.exp: Zygosity = type of conception; chorionicity = type of placentation. (Book p461)

questions.q: Fill up: Chorion is ______ membrane formed on day ______ and amnion is ______ membrane formed on day ______.
questions.exp: Chorion is the outer membrane (day 8) and amnion the inner (day 10). (Book p461)

questions.q: Dizygotic twins always have which membrane arrangement?
opts: Dichorionic diamniotic, with a separate amnion and chorion for each twin
Monochorionic diamniotic, sharing a single placental mass
Monochorionic monoamniotic, with both fetuses in one sac
Dichorionic monoamniotic, a recognised though uncommon combination
questions.exp: Dizygotic twins are always dichorionic diamniotic, since each comes from a separate ovum with its own membranes. (Book p461)

questions.q: Fill up: If the zygote splits before day 3 the result is ______ twins, whereas splitting between days 8 and 13 produces ______ twins.
questions.exp: Splitting before day 3 gives two placentas and two sacs; days 4-8 give monochorionic diamniotic; days 8-13 give monoamniotic; after day 13 the twins are conjoined. (Book p461)

questions.q: Match division timing of monozygotic zygote with membrane pattern — 1) <4 days morula 2) 4-8 days blastocyst 3) 8-12 days 4) ≥12 days … A) DCDA B) MCDA C) MCMA D) Conjoined/Siamese
questions.exp: <4 days DCDA; 4–8 days MCDA (common chorion by day 8); 8–12 days MCMA; ≥12 days conjoined twins. (Book p462)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about MCDA formation at 4-8 days is TRUE?
opts: Division at 4-8 days yields MCDA because common chorion has formed by day 8 while amnions stay separate
Division at 4-8 days yields MCDA because amnion forms before chorion so both share one sac
Division at 4-8 days yields MCDA because both chorion and amnion are shared by the two fetuses
Division at 4-8 days yields MCDA because no fetal membranes have formed at blastocyst stage
questions.exp: Division at 4-8 days (blastocyst stage) yields MCDA twins because by day 8 a common chorion is already formed while the amnions remain separate. (Book p462)

questions.q: Fill up: Division occurring after formation of single amnion, chorion and embryonic disc at ≥12 days results in ______.
questions.exp: Late division after the embryonic disc forms produces conjoined/Siamese twins. (Book p462)

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman with monochorionic monoamniotic twins at 30 weeks is counselled. Ultrasound shows cord entanglement of both cords. What is the most appropriate counselling about complications and management?
opts: Cord entanglement with sudden death of both twins; give steroids and plan caesarean at 32-34 weeks
Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome requiring laser ablation of anastomoses before 28 weeks
Preterm labour alone managed with cervical cerclage and bed rest until 38 weeks gestation
No specific risk in monoamniotic twins, so vaginal delivery at term is appropriate and safe
questions.exp: Monoamniotic twins risk cord entanglement and sudden loss, so steroids are given and delivery planned by caesarean at 32-34 weeks. (Book p462)

questions.q: Fill up: The commonest variety of twins overall is ______ and among monozygotic twins is ______.
questions.exp: The commonest variety of twins overall is DCDA (dizygotic), and among monozygotic twins it is MCDA. (Book p462)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about prognosis in twins is TRUE?
opts: Prognosis depends on chorionicity: monochorionic twins fare worse than dichorionic in every outcome
Prognosis depends on zygosity alone, since monozygotic twins do badly whatever the placentation
Prognosis depends on fetal sex, since unlike-sex twins have worst perinatal outcome overall
Prognosis depends on maternal parity, since first twin pregnancy carries poorest outlook
questions.exp: Chorionicity determines prognosis because it decides whether the circulations are shared; zygosity and sex do not. (Book p462)

questions.q: Fill up: Determination of chorionicity is best done by ______ at ______ weeks of gestation.
questions.exp: Chorionicity is best determined by transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) at 10-14 weeks in the first trimester. (Book p462)

questions.q: Match twin type with number of membrane layers — 1) DCDA 2) MCDA 3) MCMA … A) 4 layers B) 2 layers C) 0 layers
questions.exp: DCDA 4 layers, MCDA 2 layers, MCMA none. (Book p463)

questions.q: Fill up: Membrane thickness distinguishing DCDA from MCDA is ______ in DCDA vs ______ in MCDA.
questions.exp: DCDA membranes are ≥2 mm thick while MCDA are <2 mm. (Book p463)

questions.q: Match chorionicity with vascular connections — 1) Dichorionic 2) Monochorionic diamniotic 3) Monoamniotic … A) None B) Deep arteriovenous C) Superficial
questions.exp: Dichorionic placentas have no connections; monochorionic diamniotic placentas have deep arteriovenous ones, and monoamniotic placentas superficial ones. (Book p463)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about DCDA placental features is TRUE?
opts: DCDA twins have two placentas or one fused single-looking with lambda or twin-peak sign
DCDA twins have single placenta with T sign at membrane insertion site
DCDA twins have single placenta with no distinguishing ultrasound sign at all
DCDA twins have two separate placentas but always show T sign between membranes
questions.exp: Dichorionic twins have two placentas, or a fused single-looking one, and always show the lambda or twin-peak sign. (Book p463)

questions.q: Fill up: The T sign on USG, with single chorion and no intervening placenta, indicates ______.
questions.exp: T sign = single chorion without intervening placenta = MCDA. (Book p463)

questions.q: Match twin type with its specific complications — 1) MCDA 2) MCMA … A) TTTS, TAPS, selective IUGR B) Cord entanglement and conjoined twins
questions.exp: MCDA twins specifically risk TTTS through deep vascular connections; MCMA twins specifically risk cord entanglement. (Book p463)

questions.q: Fill up: Delivery timing is ______ for DCDA, ______ for MCDA and ______ for MCMA twins.
questions.exp: Delivery timing is 38 weeks for DCDA twins, 36 weeks for MCDA twins, and 32-34 weeks by caesarean after corticosteroids for MCMA twins. (Book p463)

questions.sec: DCDA vs MCDA vs MCMA & conjoined twins
questions.q: Match the ultrasound sign with what it means — 1) Lambda or twin-peak sign 2) T sign 3) Conjoined twins … A) A wedge of placenta between the membranes, which indicates dichorionicity B) The intertwin membrane meeting the placenta at a right angle with no placental tissue between, indicating monochorionicity C) Splitting after day 13, so the fetuses share tissue and often share organs
questions.exp: The lambda sign proves dichorionicity in the first trimester, the T sign proves monochorionicity, and conjoined twins follow very late splitting. (Book p463)

questions.sec: USG in twin pregnancy & conjoined twins
questions.q: USG in twin pregnancy is significant for assessing gestational age, chorionicity and ↑NT. Chorionicity can be determined earliest at ______ and best at ______.
questions.exp: Chorionicity: earliest 7 weeks, best 10 weeks. (Book p464)

questions.sec: USG in twin pregnancy & conjoined twins
questions.q: An increased nuchal translucency in a twin pregnancy raises suspicion of ______, and its ideal assessment time is the ______ trimester.
questions.exp: ↑NT suggests TTTS; the ideal time is the 2nd trimester. (Book p464)

questions.sec: USG in twin pregnancy & conjoined twins
questions.q: Which is NOT a marker of dichorionicity on USG?
questions.exp: Dichorionicity markers: ≥4 membranes, ≥2 mm thickness, different sexes, 2 placentae and twin peak sign. (Book p464)

questions.sec: USG in twin pregnancy & conjoined twins
questions.q: Conjoined twins are a complication of which twin type, and how are the types named?
opts: Monoamniotic twins; parapagus, thoracophagus, rachiphagus and craniophagus
Dichorionic twins, in whom only cephalopagus has ever been described
Monochorionic diamniotic twins, in whom only ischiopagus is described
Dizygotic twins, in whom only parapagus joining has been recorded
questions.exp: Conjoined twins follow splitting after day 13, so they are monoamniotic and monochorionic; the types are named for the shared part. (Book p464)

questions.sec: USG in twin pregnancy & conjoined twins
questions.q: Management of conjoined twins is:
opts: Caesarean at 32-34 weeks after completing a steroid course
Vaginal delivery at 38 weeks after completing a steroid course
Fetal reduction at 12 weeks, then delivery at 38 weeks
Serial amnioreduction, then delivery at 34 completed weeks
questions.exp: Conjoined twins are managed by caesarean section between 32 and 34 weeks after completing the steroid course. (Book p464)

questions.q: Maternal complications of twin pregnancy include pronounced haemodynamic changes, ↑ placental size, polyhydramnios and which liver conditions?
opts: Intrahepatic cholestasis and acute fatty liver of pregnancy
Cirrhosis and acute hepatitis E infection in pregnancy
Gilbert syndrome and Dubin-Johnson syndrome in pregnancy
Budd-Chiari syndrome and portal vein thrombosis in pregnancy
questions.exp: Maternal complications of twin pregnancy include pronounced haemodynamic changes, increased placental size, polyhydramnios, and the liver conditions intrahepatic cholestasis and acute fatty liver of pregnancy. (Book p465)

questions.q: Twin pregnancy increases the risk of which obstetric complications?
opts: Preterm labour, pre-eclampsia, postpartum haemorrhage, cord prolapse and malpresentation
Gestational diabetes alone, with no effect on the course of labour or delivery
Hyperemesis gravidarum alone, with no increase in risk later in the pregnancy
Iron deficiency anaemia alone, since only the maternal blood volume is affected
questions.exp: Overdistension of the uterus and a large placental mass explain the whole spectrum of increased obstetric risk in twins. (Book p465)

questions.q: ↑ hCG and ↑ human placental lactogen in twins explain which associations?
questions.exp: ↑hCG → hyperemesis; ↑hPL → gestational diabetes. (Book p465)

questions.q: Pre-eclampsia in twin pregnancy is attributed to:
questions.exp: The notes attribute pre-eclampsia to increased paternal antigen exposure. (Book p465)

questions.q: PIH prophylaxis in twin pregnancy uses:
opts: Low-dose aspirin 80-150 mg/day started before 16 weeks, ideally 12
High-dose aspirin 300 mg/day started after 28 weeks
Calcium supplementation only, started after 20 weeks
Low-molecular-weight heparin from the time of conception
questions.exp: PIH prophylaxis in twin pregnancy uses low-dose aspirin 80-150 mg/day started before 16 weeks, ideally at 12 weeks. (Book p465)

questions.q: Fetal complications are m/c in which order?
opts: Monochorionic worse than dichorionic, and monozygotic worse than dizygotic, apart from cumulative chromosomal risk
Dichorionic twins do worse than monochorionic twins in every respect
Dizygotic twins always do worse than monozygotic twins
All types carry exactly the same risk of fetal complications
questions.exp: Shared circulation drives risk, so monochorionic and monozygotic twins do worse; dizygotic twins carry two independent chromosomal risks instead. (Book p465)

questions.q: For aneuploidy testing, sampling differs by zygosity how?
opts: Monozygotic – sample any one twin; dizygotic – sample both twins
Monozygotic – sample both; dizygotic – sample one
questions.exp: Monozygotic twins share genetics so one sample suffices; dizygotic need both sampled. (Book p465)

questions.q: Prognosis depends on chorionicity and amnionicity EXCEPT for which two complications?
opts: Preterm labour (related to number of twins) and IUGR
questions.exp: Preterm labour relates to twin number and IUGR is independent of chorionicity. (Book p465)

questions.q: Fetal reduction in multifetal pregnancy: DOC, target and timing are:
opts: Intracardiac KCl injection into the fetus with least chance of survival, at 10–13 weeks
Intracardiac KCl into the largest fetus at 20 weeks
Aspiration of amniotic fluid at 8 weeks
questions.exp: Intracardiac KCl to the least-viable fetus at 10–13 weeks; it does not affect the other fetus's survival. (Book p465)

questions.q: All of the following are maternal complications that are commoner in twin pregnancy EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Twin pregnancies are delivered early; the others are all more frequent because of the larger placental mass and greater hormonal load. (Book p465)

questions.q: The three complications common to ALL twin pregnancies are:
opts: Preterm labour (m/c), IUGR and congenital anomalies
Cord prolapse, vasa previa and rupture
questions.exp: Preterm labour (m/c), IUGR and congenital anomalies affect all twins. (Book p466)

questions.q: In a primigravida twin pregnancy without history of preterm labour or 2nd-trimester abortion, cervical cerclage is:
questions.exp: The notes state cerclage is not done in this scenario. (Book p466)

questions.q: Congenital anomalies in twins are m/c compared with singletons and follow which pattern?
opts: Twin above singleton; monochorionic above dichorionic; heart defects
Singleton above twin; dichorionic above monochorionic
Dichorionic above monochorionic; neural tube defects only
Twin above singleton; monochorionic above dichorionic; renal defects
questions.exp: Congenital anomalies are commoner in twins than singletons, commoner in monochorionic than dichorionic twins, and heart defects predominate. (Book p466)

questions.q: For TTTS screening in monochorionic twins, echocardiography is done at ______ and a target/anomaly/level II scan is done in ______.
questions.exp: Echo at 18–22 weeks; the level II scan applies to all pregnant women. (Book p466)

questions.q: Vanishing twin syndrome refers to ______ and is common in ______.
opts: Early spontaneous reduction of a twin pregnancy to singleton; IVF pregnancies
Death of both twins at term; spontaneous conception
Late IUD of one twin; natural conception
questions.exp: Vanishing twin = early spontaneous reduction to singleton, common after IVF. (Book p466)

questions.q: Effect of a vanishing twin on the surviving co-twin:
questions.exp: The second twin usually survives normally, ± LBW/SGA. (Book p466)

questions.q: After death of one twin, complications in the survivor depend on chorionicity how?
opts: Monochorionic survivors are at risk through the shared anastomoses; dichorionic survivors largely are not
Both monochorionic and dichorionic survivors are at equal risk of neurological injury
Dichorionic survivors are at greater risk, because the second placenta also fails
Neither twin is at any risk once one of them has died in utero
questions.exp: Acute transfusion through anastomoses at the moment of death is what injures the monochorionic survivor's brain. (Book p466)

questions.q: In a dying monochorionic co-twin, the sequence in twin A (high-pressure system) flowing to twin B (low-pressure system) causes:
opts: Twin A becomes hypotensive and anaemic, exsanguinating into the low-pressure twin
Twin A becomes polycythaemic as blood flows in from the dying co-twin
Twin B becomes hypertensive from the sudden increase in blood volume
No haemodynamic change occurs in either twin at the moment of death
questions.exp: When the monochorionic co-twin dies, the survivor's low-pressure circulation drains the dying twin, which is how the survivor is injured. (Book p466)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about single intrauterine death in a twin pregnancy is TRUE?
opts: In monochorionic twins the survivor risks neurological injury from acute inter-twin transfusion, while in dichorionic twins the main risk is preterm delivery
Death of a dichorionic co-twin is more dangerous to the survivor than death of a monochorionic co-twin
Immediate delivery is mandatory whenever one twin dies, whatever the gestation
Maternal disseminated intravascular coagulation appears within hours in a third of these pregnancies
questions.exp: Vascular anastomoses make monochorionic loss dangerous to the survivor's brain; maternal coagulopathy is rare and immediate delivery is not always best. (Book p466)

questions.q: Management when USG shows impending death of the 1st twin:
questions.exp: Impending death of the 1st twin mandates immediate delivery of both. (Book p467)

questions.q: The four complications specific to monochorionic twins are:
opts: TTTS, TAPS, TRAP and selective IUGR
Cord entanglement, conjoining, vanishing twin, show
questions.exp: TTTS, TAPS, TRAP and selective IUGR are monochorionic-specific. (Book p467)

questions.q: Differentiate IUGR from selective IUGR in twins.
opts: Ordinary IUGR affects both twins; selective IUGR is monochorionic, one normal and one growth-restricted twin
The two terms mean exactly the same thing and are interchangeable
Selective IUGR is a complication confined to dichorionic twins
Ordinary IUGR affects only one twin of the pair
questions.exp: Selective growth restriction is a monochorionic problem of unequal placental sharing, with one twin normally grown. (Book p467)

questions.q: TTTS occurs due to:
opts: Deep vascular anastomosis between artery and vein
questions.exp: Deep arterio-venous anastomoses cause TTTS. (Book p467)

questions.q: Prevalence of TTTS by chorionicity/amnionicity:
opts: Commonest in monochorionic diamniotic twins, least common in monoamniotic, and not seen in dichorionic twins
Commonest in dichorionic twins with two separate placentas, and never seen in monochorionic twins
Commonest in monoamniotic twins because of cord entanglement, and never in monochorionic diamniotic twins
Equally common in every type, since transfusion depends on cord insertion rather than chorionicity
questions.exp: Deep arteriovenous anastomoses in monochorionic diamniotic placentas drive TTTS; without shared circulation the syndrome cannot occur. (Book p467)

questions.q: In TTTS, the DONOR twin shows which renal and fluid findings?
opts: ↓ renal blood flow (↑ renal failure risk), ↓ GFR and oligohydramnios
questions.exp: The donor has reduced renal perfusion and GFR with oligohydramnios; the recipient the opposite. (Book p467)

questions.q: Haemoglobin consequences in TTTS are:
opts: Donor: anaemia with heart failure — recipient: polycythaemia with thrombosis and failure
Donor: polycythaemia with thrombosis — recipient: anaemia and heart failure
Both twins become anaemic from the unbalanced transfusion
Both twins become polycythaemic from the shared circulation
questions.exp: The donor is volume depleted and anaemic; the recipient is volume loaded and polycythaemic, with thrombotic and cardiac complications. (Book p467)

questions.q: Peak systolic velocity of the MCA in TTTS donor vs recipient:
questions.exp: MCA-PSV ≥1.5 MoM in the anemic donor and <0.8 MoM in the polycythemic recipient. (Book p467)

questions.q: Serious complications listed for TTTS fetuses are:
questions.exp: Hydrops fetalis and death are the listed complications. (Book p467)

questions.q: Fill up: Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome is driven by ______ anastomoses in a monochorionic placenta, and the donor twin becomes ______.
opts: arteriovenous; oliguric with oligohydramnios and growth restriction
questions.exp: Unidirectional arteriovenous anastomoses make the donor hypovolaemic with oliguria and oligohydramnios, and the recipient hypervolaemic with polyhydramnios. (Book p467)

questions.q: The best method for amniotic fluid assessment in twin pregnancy is:
opts: Single largest vertical pocket on USG
Amniotic fluid index summing four quadrants
questions.exp: The single largest vertical pocket is the best method in twins. (Book p468)

questions.q: Diagnostic criteria of TTTS in monochorionic diamniotic twins:
opts: Polyhydramnios in one twin with oligohydramnios in the other
questions.exp: Poly-oligo sequence between MCDA twins defines TTTS. (Book p468)

questions.q: The early marker of TTTS is:
questions.exp: Increased NT is the early marker of TTTS. (Book p468)

questions.q: The 'stuck twin' appearance in TTTS results from:
opts: Renin-angiotensin activation in the donor, causing oliguria, anuria and anhydramnios
Polyhydramnios in the recipient compressing the donor against the uterine wall
Cord entanglement between the two fetuses lying in a single sac
A uterine septum separating the two gestational sacs
questions.exp: The donor twin is volume depleted, activates the renin-angiotensin system and stops making urine, so it becomes the stuck twin in an anhydramniotic sac. (Book p468)

questions.q: Quintero stage 1 vs stage 2 of TTTS differ by:
opts: Stage 1: the donor bladder is still visible — stage 2: it is not visible, and Doppler is normal in both
Stage 1: the Doppler is already abnormal — stage 2: the Doppler becomes normal again
Stage 2: hydrops fetalis is already present in the recipient twin
Stage 2: one or both twins have already died in utero
questions.exp: Quintero stage 1 still shows a donor bladder; stage 2 loses it, while abnormal Doppler belongs to stage 3 and hydrops to stage 4. (Book p468)

questions.q: Match Quintero stages 3, 4 and 5.
opts: Stage 3 abnormal Doppler; stage 4 hydrops fetalis in one/both; stage 5 death of one/both twins
Stage 3 hydrops; stage 4 abnormal Doppler; stage 5 anuria
Stage 3 anuria; stage 4 Doppler; stage 5 hydrops
Stage 3 death; stage 4 hydrops; stage 5 Doppler
questions.exp: Stages 3–5 add abnormal Doppler, hydrops and death respectively. (Book p468)

questions.q: At 20 weeks a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy has a deepest vertical pocket of 8.5 cm in one sac and 1.5 cm in the other, and a bladder is visible in both fetuses. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Refer for fetoscopic laser ablation of the placental anastomoses
Reassure her and repeat the scan in four weeks, since both bladders are visible
Immediate delivery, since this is advanced disease
Serial amnioreduction alone, because laser offers no advantage
questions.exp: Oligo-polyhydramnios with both bladders visible is Quintero stage II, and laser ablation of anastomoses is the definitive treatment before 26 weeks. (Book p468)

questions.q: Follow-up Doppler studies in monochorionic twins are done at 16–20 weeks and include:
opts: Umbilical artery, vein, ductus venosus and PSV of MCA
questions.exp: Doppler at 16–20 weeks covers umbilical artery/vein, ductus venosus and MCA-PSV. (Book p469)

questions.q: USG follow-up in TTTS-risk twins assesses:
opts: Fetal biometry, liquor volume in each sac and Doppler for hydrops and abnormal waveforms
Cervical length alone, since transfusion does not affect growth or liquor volume
Placental grading alone, which predicts transfusion before any fetal change appears
Fetal sex determination alone, since chorionicity is already known from the first scan
questions.exp: Surveillance looks for the consequences of unbalanced transfusion: growth discordance, liquor discordance, abnormal Doppler and hydrops. (Book p469)

questions.q: Echocardiography of the RECIPIENT twin in TTTS looks for:
opts: Pulmonary stenosis or atresia, ventricular hypertrophy and predominantly right-sided dysfunction
Left ventricular hypoplasia with a small aortic root and coarctation
An isolated ventricular septal defect with no myocardial hypertrophy at all
A structurally and functionally normal heart in the great majority of recipient twins
questions.exp: The recipient twin is volume loaded, so the right side bears the brunt: pulmonary stenosis or atresia, hypertrophy and right-sided dysfunction. (Book p469)

questions.q: Treatment of TTTS by gestational age: ≤28 weeks vs >28 weeks.
opts: Fetoscopic laser ablation of vascular anastomoses; serial amnioreduction
questions.exp: ≤28 weeks fetoscopic laser ablation; >28 weeks serial amnioreduction. (Book p469)

questions.q: TAPS is best described as:
opts: A chronic form of twin-to-twin transfusion through tiny anastomoses, with anaemia and polycythaemia but no fluid discordance
An acute severe form of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome with sudden polyhydramnios in both sacs
A complication confined to dichorionic twins in which one placenta has a velamentous cord insertion
A complication of cord entanglement in monoamniotic twins that causes sudden death of both twins
questions.exp: TAPS is chronic slow transfusion through anastomoses under 1 mm: the haemoglobin gap is large but the liquor volumes stay normal. (Book p469)

questions.q: TAPS can occur spontaneously or after which procedure?
questions.exp: TAPS may follow laser ablation of TTTS. (Book p469)

questions.q: Features of TAPS: haemoglobin, amniotic fluid and MCA-PSV.
opts: Donor anaemia and recipient polycythaemia, with normal liquor volume in both sacs
An oligo-polyhydramnios sequence, with equal peak systolic velocities
Donor polycythaemia together with anaemia in the recipient
Abnormal liquor volume in both sacs from the very beginning
questions.exp: TAPS is defined by a large haemoglobin difference without the liquor discordance of classic twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome. (Book p469)

questions.q: TRAP sequence is a rare complication of monochorionic twins caused by:
opts: An aberrant artery-to-artery anastomosis through which the pump twin perfuses the acardiac twin in reverse
Deep arteriovenous anastomoses of the kind that produce classic twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome
Superficial venous anastomoses that allow a slow transfusion between the two circulations
Complete absence of any anastomosis, so each twin keeps an entirely separate circulation
questions.exp: TRAP needs an artery-to-artery anastomosis: deoxygenated blood from the pump twin reaches the acardiac twin first and stunts its development. (Book p469)

questions.q: Match the monochorionic complication with its description — 1) TRAP sequence 2) Twin anaemia-polycythaemia sequence 3) Selective fetal growth restriction … A) An acardiac twin perfused in reverse through artery-to-artery anastomoses B) Chronic slow transfusion producing a large inter-twin haemoglobin difference without the oligo-polyhydramnios sequence C) One twin below the third centile with abnormal Doppler from unequal placental sharing
questions.exp: TRAP has a perfused acardiac twin, TAPS shows a haemoglobin gap without fluid discordance, and selective growth restriction reflects placental share. (Book p469)

questions.q: Outcomes in the acardiac twin of TRAP are named:
opts: Acardiac acephalus (lower body developed); acardiac amorphous (no formed parts)
Acardiac acephalus (lower body developed); acardiac anceps (head formed only)
Acardiac amorphous (no formed parts); acardiac acephalus (lower body developed)
Acardiac anceps (head formed only); acardiac amorphous (no formed parts)
questions.exp: Outcomes in the acardiac twin of TRAP are acardiac acephalus, in which only the lower part is developed, and acardiac amorphus, an amorphous mass with no formed parts. (Book p470)

questions.q: Selective IUGR is defined by fetal weight < 10th percentile of the normal co-twin OR:
questions.exp: Discordance >25% in weight also defines selective IUGR. (Book p470)

questions.q: Causes of selective IUGR listed are:
opts: Unequal placental sharing and unequal splitting of the cell mass
Deep vascular anastomoses with artery-to-artery connections
Maternal diabetes causing symmetrical overgrowth of both twins
Cord entanglement restricting blood flow to one twin only
questions.exp: The listed causes of selective IUGR are unequal placental sharing and unequal splitting of the initial cell mass. (Book p470)

questions.q: Complications specific to MONOAMNIOTIC twins and the cause of cord entanglement:
opts: Cord entanglement and conjoined twins; true knots form the cause
TTTS and TAPS, caused by the deep vascular anastomoses
Selective IUGR, from unequal sharing of the placental mass
A vanishing twin, from thrombosis of the shared umbilical cord
questions.exp: Complications specific to monoamniotic twins are cord entanglement and conjoined twins, with true knots forming the cause of the entanglement. (Book p470)

questions.q: Management of monoamniotic twins with cord entanglement risk:
questions.exp: C-section at 32–34 weeks is advised. (Book p470)

questions.q: The 1st twin is defined as the one that:
opts: Is closer to the internal os during pregnancy / comes out first during delivery
Is labelled by the sonologist arbitrarily
questions.exp: The twin closer to the internal os (delivered first) is the 1st twin. (Book p471)

questions.q: The m/c and 2nd m/c presentation combinations in twins are:
questions.exp: Both-vertex is m/c; 1st vertex + 2nd breech is second m/c. (Book p471)

questions.q: Interlocking of twins is seen with which combination and is managed by:
questions.exp: Interlocking occurs when the 1st is breech and 2nd cephalic; C-section is done. (Book p471)

questions.q: Mode of delivery in twins depends on the presentation of the:
opts: The first twin: a vertex first twin allows vaginal delivery whatever the second twin is doing
The second twin: any non-vertex second twin means both babies are delivered by caesarean section
The larger twin: whichever twin weighs more determines whether a caesarean is needed
The placental site: an anterior placenta makes a vaginal delivery of twins impossible
questions.exp: The presentation of the first twin governs the plan; a breech or transverse second twin can often still be delivered vaginally by an expert. (Book p471)

questions.q: Match delivery plans when the 1st twin is vertex: 2nd vertex, 2nd breech, 2nd transverse.
opts: Second vertex: vaginal delivery — second breech: assisted breech — second transverse: internal podalic version in theatre
Every combination is delivered by caesarean section once the first twin has been born vaginally
Every combination can be delivered vaginally by an experienced operator without preparation
Caesarean section for a breech second twin only, since version is never attempted for a transverse lie
questions.exp: When the first twin is vertex, a vertex or breech second twin can usually be delivered vaginally, and a transverse second twin by version and breech extraction. (Book p471)

questions.q: After delivery of the 1st twin, which drug is contraindicated and why?
opts: Methylergometrine, since it contracts the uterus and traps the second twin
Oxytocin, since it causes maternal hypotension at this stage
Misoprostol, since it causes pyrexia at this stage of labour
Magnesium sulfate, since it causes maternal sedation and drowsiness
questions.exp: After delivery of the first twin, methylergometrine is contraindicated because it causes uterine contractions that trap the second twin. (Book p471)

questions.q: The maximum acceptable time gap between delivery of the twins is ______; beyond it the action is ______.
opts: 30 minutes; immediate C-section of the 2nd twin
questions.exp: A gap >30 minutes mandates immediate C-section of the second twin. (Book p471)

questions.q: Internal podalic version has a single indication and one contraindication:
opts: 2nd twin in transverse lie; previous h/o C-section
questions.exp: IPV is indicated only for a transverse 2nd twin and c/i after previous C-section. (Book p471)

questions.q: Technique of internal podalic version:
opts: Under general anaesthesia a hand is passed into the uterus, the feet are grasped and the fetus is turned to a breech
Under spinal anaesthesia the head is rotated with forceps before delivery
External manipulation through the abdomen with the membranes left intact
Traction on the cord under continuous ultrasound guidance in the labour ward
questions.exp: Internal podalic version is an intrauterine manoeuvre under general anaesthesia, grasping a foot and converting the lie to a breech. (Book p471)

questions.q: The note adds that EXTERNAL cephalic version is attempted only if:
opts: The fetus is breech at 30 weeks
questions.exp: ECV requires intact membranes per the note. (Book p471)

questions.q: Fill up: Uncomplicated dichorionic diamniotic twins are delivered at about ______ weeks, whereas uncomplicated monochorionic diamniotic twins are delivered at about ______ weeks.
questions.exp: Monochorionic twins are delivered earlier because of the unpredictable risk from anastomoses and late single fetal death. (Book p471)

units.title: Dizygotic vs monozygotic twins → Superfecundation, superfetation & risk factors
units.guide: Contrast dizygotic and monozygotic twins from formation to fingerprints, apply Hellin's rule and separate superfecundation from superfetation with their risk factors. Focus for this checkpoint: Dizygotic vs monozygotic twins, Superfecundation, superfetation & risk factors.

units.title: Chorionicity & amnionicity
units.guide: Time the zygote's division against membrane formation to predict DCDA, MCDA, MCMA or conjoined twins, and know why chorionicity drives prognosis and scan timing. Focus for this checkpoint: Chorionicity & amnionicity.

units.title: DCDA vs MCDA vs MCMA → USG in twin pregnancy & conjoined twins
units.sec: DCDA vs MCDA vs MCMA & twin USG · p463-464
units.guide: Read the membrane-layer, thickness, vascular-connection and lambda/T-sign table, then use twin ultrasound markers and conjoined-twin management. Focus for this checkpoint: DCDA vs MCDA vs MCMA, USG in twin pregnancy & conjoined twins.

units.title: Maternal complications & PIH prophylaxis → Fetal complications & fetal reduction
units.guide: List the exaggerated maternal physiology of twins, aspirin prophylaxis for PIH and the rules of aneuploidy sampling and fetal reduction. Focus for this checkpoint: Maternal complications & PIH prophylaxis, Fetal complications & fetal reduction.

units.title: Complications common to all twins → Death of one twin
units.sec: Common complications & death of one twin · p466-467
units.guide: Remember the three universal twin complications, the vanishing twin and the haemodynamic fate of a surviving monochorionic co-twin. Focus for this checkpoint: Complications common to all twins, Death of one twin.

units.title: Monochorionic-specific complications → etiopathogenesis & donor-recipient
units.guide: Distinguish selective IUGR from general IUGR and build the TTTS donor-recipient picture from anastomosis depth to MCA-PSV. Focus for this checkpoint: Monochorionic-specific complications, TTTS: etiopathogenesis & donor-recipient.

units.title: diagnosis & staging → follow-up & treatment
units.guide: Apply the poly-oligo criteria, stuck-twin physiology and Quintero stages, then choose laser ablation versus serial amnioreduction by gestational age. Focus for this checkpoint: TTTS: diagnosis & staging, TTTS: follow-up & treatment.

units.title: TAPS & TRAP → Selective IUGR & monoamniotic complications
units.guide: Separate TAPS from TTTS by normal fluid volumes, trace the acardiac twin of TRAP and manage cord entanglement in monoamniotic pregnancies. Focus for this checkpoint: TAPS & TRAP, Selective IUGR & monoamniotic complications.

units.title: Delivery in twin pregnancy
units.guide: Let the first twin's presentation decide the route, handle the transverse second twin with internal podalic version and respect the 30-minute gap rule. Focus for this checkpoint: Delivery in twin pregnancy.
